title: XI: The Interior of a Heart

teacherSummary.text: Dimmesdale's suffering makes him a more powerful preacher; his people revere him more as he calls himself vile. He fasts, keeps vigils and scourges himself in a locked closet, sees visions, and cannot confess.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “He had spoken the very truth, and transformed it into the veriest falsehood” slowly and put it in my own words: Dimmesdale tells his congregation that he is a vile sinner, but they take his words as proof of his holy humility. Next, craft. I notice the paradox "spoken the very truth, and transformed it into the veriest falsehood," which sets truth and lie side by side. The strongest word is “falsehood”: it shows how a true statement, made vaguely, becomes a lie. Then, effect. Why does Dimmesdale's public confession make his guilt worse? My answer: Because he never names his sin, his "confession" only raises his reputation; he knows it, so each sermon deepens his self-hatred and his hypocrisy.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Dimmesdale scourges himself, fasts and keeps sleepless vigils out of guilt. Treat this as self-harm with care: do not dwell on details, and remind students that support is available.
